svg.title: AI-based access control architecture
svg.desc:
Two phases, separated in time.
Access rules generation time, which runs on an onboarding event and on a role change. The Identity Provider Pod (Keycloak) holds the Service Provider (SPI) listener and the Admin API, which serves users, roles and clients. The SPI listener publishes each change to NATS JetStream in the Event Broker Pod, which notifies the AIAC Agent in the Agent Pod. The AIAC Agent also reads the access control policy. It works out the smallest set of PolicyRules for the affected workload: who can access the new workload, and what the new workload can access. It calls an OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint to propose and audit the rules; that is the only model call. The AIAC Agent reads roles, scopes and clients from the IdP Configuration Service in the Rossoctl Interface Pod, which calls the Admin API over admin REST. The Policy Computation Engine in the Agent Pod merges the rules into the model, stores it in the Policy Model Store Pod, and applies it through the PDP Policy Writer (OPA), which renders the Rego and writes the AuthorizationPolicy custom resource on the Kubernetes API. The Kubernetes API and bundle-service sit outside AIAC. bundle-service reads the Rego from that resource and composes one bundle for each pod.
Request time, which runs on each call. A caller (a user or an agent) reaches the OPA plugin in the AuthBridge gate of an agent or tool pod, which runs an inbound chain and an outbound chain. The plugin asks OPA. OPA evaluates the Rego bundle that it polls from bundle-service, and answers allow or deny. On allow, the call reaches the agent or tool container.
